items.title: This burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadly | Sadiq Khan
items.blurb:
Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth

  • Report: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oil

Europe is burning. This summer, an unprecedented series of heatwaves has swept through the continent and across many parts of the globe. The consequences have been nothing short of catastrophic. In recent weeks deadly blazes have torn through France, Greece and Spain, killing firefighters, forcing people from their homes and robbing them of their livelihoods.

With Tuesday marking Britain’s 34th day of temperatures exceeding 30C (86F) this year, the UK has also found itself reckoning with ferocious heat. Wildfires have forced evacuations in Suffolk and the Cairngorms. In London – where parks have become burnt, brittle and brown – hundreds of grass fires have put our firefighters under pressure like never before. In July, the weather station at Kew Gardens recorded its first ever month without rain since it started operating in 1871. As rivers run dry and reservoirs run low, farmers are warning of food shortages amid the deepening drought. With thousands of deaths already estimated to be linked to the extreme heat we saw in May and June alone, it’s likely this figure will climb higher still.

When Maduka Okoye visited Paris fashion week for the Jean Paul Gaultier show, taking his seat in the front row alongside rapper Cardi B, the online reaction was swift. Within hours, footage of the Udinese and Nigeria goalkeeper was all over TikTok and Instagram – where his audience now stretches near to two million followers – transforming the appearance into a viral cultural moment that crossed beyond the boundaries of football.

Yet ask Okoye to reflect on his sudden explosion into the fashion ecosystem, and he frames it not as a pursuit of celebrity or status, but as a genuine interest in art. “Being at the Paris fashion week was really impressive,” Okoye tells the Guardian. “It was my first time really coming into contact with high fashion, and it was fascinating. It’s a true art form. I enjoyed it immensely, and since that moment I’ve become a much bigger fan of fashion than I was before.”

items.title: NIT Team Develops Unique Way to Clean Solar Panels Using AI to Save Water & Money
items.blurb: Solar panels need sunlight to work well. But in many parts of India, dust, bird droppings and pollution can quickly build up on their surface and block that sunlight. For large solar farms in dry and dusty regions, keeping thousands of panels clean is a constant task. Dirt can reduce the amount of electricity the panels generate, while regular cleaning can use large amounts of water and require significant manpower. Researchers at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Rourkela have now developed an Artificial Intelligence-powered system that could make this process far more targeted. The system can monitor solar panels, identify which ones need cleaning and focus only on those areas. This could help solar plants use less water and labour while keeping panels working efficiently. An AI system that knows when cleaning is needed The technology has been developed by Prof. Arun Kumar, Assistant Professor, Prof. Bibhudatta Sahoo, Professor, and research graduates Dr Lopamudra Hota and Dr Biraja Prasad Nayak from the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at NIT Rourkela. The team has secured an Indian patent titled “Federated Learning-based Autonomous System and Method for Monitoring and Cleaning Solar Plant”. The patented system combines AI, federated learning and autonomous cleaning to help solar plants reduce unnecessary water use, labour and maintenance costs. Photograph: ( Nevron Express ) The problem they are trying to solve is becoming increasingly important as India adds more solar power capacity. According to the researchers, solar farms in dry and dusty areas can lose up to 40% of their energy generation because of dust, bird droppings, industrial pollutants and other material settling on the panels. Cleaning these panels regularly brings its own challenges. Many existing systems depend heavily on labour and water. Solar farms also often clean panels according to a fixed schedule, whether every panel needs cleaning or not. This can mean spending time, money and water cleaning panels that are already working well. So, how does the system work? The NIT Rourkela team has developed a system that uses Artificial Intelligence to continuously check the condition of solar panels. It can detect faults, study real-time conditions and recommend which panels actually need cleaning. So instead of cleaning an entire solar farm at fixed intervals, operators could focus only on the panels that need attention. The system uses a type of AI called Federated Learning, or FL. In simple terms, Federated Learning allows different devices or systems to learn from data without sending all the original information to one central server. Instead of cleaning every panel on a fixed schedule, the technology monitors real-time conditions to identify which panels actually need attention. Photograph: ( Aajjo ) The technology has so far been tested through simulations and is currently at Technology Readiness Level 3, or TRL-3 . This means the basic idea has been demonstrated as a proof of concept under controlled experimental conditions. Keeping solar plant data protected Another important part of the system is the way it handles data. Many conventional AI systems collect raw information from different locations and send it to a central server for processing. The NIT Rourkela system follows a different approach. It uses a privacy-preserving Federated Learning architecture, where encrypted information is shared instead of raw operational data. The researchers say this approach can reduce concerns around data privacy, cybersecurity and the amount of internet bandwidth required. It could also make the technology easier to scale across larger solar installations. Speaking about the technology, Dr Arun Kumar, Assistant Professor at NIT Rourkela, said, “The patented system combines federated learning, edge computing, artificial intelligence, autonomous cleaning, and predictive maintenance into a single integrated sandbox platform.” He added that features such as real-time intelligence, automatic fault detection, selective cleaning, lower water use and reduced maintenance costs make the system unique. Where could this technology be used? The researchers say the system could work across many different types of solar installations. These include large utility-scale solar power plants, floating solar farms, rooftop solar systems, industrial solar parks, smart city energy infrastructure, defence installations and remote off-grid renewable energy systems. Once scaled, the technology is expected to offer better performance at around 10% of the cost of existing systems Photograph: ( Electrical India ) This means the technology could eventually be useful for both large energy producers and smaller renewable energy networks looking to reduce the effort and cost involved in maintaining solar panels. Could it make solar cleaning cheaper too? The researchers also believe the technology could significantly reduce the cost of maintaining solar panels. Prof. Bibhudatta Sahoo of NIT Rourkela says many existing solutions come with high upfront costs and offer limited intelligence. Their system, he says, brings several AI-based functions together so that monitoring, decision-making and cleaning can happen more automatically. “While current market solutions suffer from high capital costs and limited intelligence, our developed system integrates advanced AI capabilities for autonomous operation,” he said. Once developed for large-scale field use, the researchers expect the system to offer its features at around 10% of the cost of existing systems . From AI-powered monitoring to autonomous cleaning, the team hopes to make solar maintenance smarter, leaner and more sustainable Photograph: ( Solar Square ) What happens next? So far, the system has been tested through simulations. The team’s next step is to build a physical hardware prototype and connect it with Internet of Things, or IoT, sensors . These sensors would help collect information directly from solar installations and allow the researchers to test how the system performs outside the laboratory. The team plans to move from simulation-based testing to pilot projects in real-world conditions. They are also looking to work with government agencies and industry partners to support field testing and eventually transfer the technology for wider use. Future versions of the system could include drones for inspecting solar panels, multiple cleaning machines working together and AI tools that can predict how much energy a solar plant is likely to generate. Helping solar farms get more from every panel India is expanding its solar energy infrastructure as part of its National Solar Mission and its larger Net Zero goals. As more solar farms are built, keeping them efficient without using excessive water, labour and money will become an important part of the challenge. The NIT Rourkela team’s system aims to make that maintenance more intelligent by checking which panels need attention and focusing cleaning where it is actually required. If the technology performs successfully in real-world trials and is eventually used at scale, it could help solar plants generate more power while using fewer resources.

items.title: A Day in the Life of a Farmer Who Patrols Elephant Corridors All Night to Protect Crops
items.blurb: By the time the last cooking fires die down in the villages bordering Uttar Pradesh's Katarniaghat forests, another workday is only just beginning. Around 10.30 pm, after spending the day tending to crops, feeding cattle and finishing household chores, a group of farmers gathers on the edge of the village. They pull reflective jackets over dust-covered shirts, test the batteries in their torches, sling whistles around their necks and check that the megaphones still work. No one knows how long the night will last. Some nights, they return home before midnight. On others, they remain awake until sunrise, tracking elephants moving through fields where sugarcane grows barely a few metres from the forest. Their task is not to drive the animals away. It is to ensure that both the elephants and the people sharing this landscape make it safely through the night. This is what a day looks like for the Gajmitras of Katarniaghat. A community-led rapid response network that has become one of India's most effective examples of people and elephants learning to share the same landscape. Elephants remember the routes across the India-Nepal border The villages lie within the Terai Arc Landscape, a transboundary conservation landscape stretching across northern India and southern Nepal. Dense sal forests, wetlands and riverine grasslands link Dudhwa Tiger Reserve with Nepal's Bardia National Park, allowing elephants to move across the international border as they have for generations. The Gajmitras are the first line of response whenever elephants approach human settlements. Photograph: (Sitangshu Das) But political boundaries mean little to an elephant. Elephants remember migration routes and ancient pathways for decades, aided by a large hippocampus in the brain. The oldest female leader, the matriarch, guides the family herd across hundreds of kilometres to hidden waterholes, safe paths and food sources using this spatial memory. They seem to live up to the famous saying that they "never forget". The hippocampus is the part of the brain that handles memory and spatial navigation, helping them remember routes and survival information for years. So long before villages, roads and sugarcane fields emerged, these seasonal migration routes already existed. Around 50 to 150 wild elephants, many migrating across the transboundary corridor from Nepal, now inhabit the Katarniaghat Wildlife Sanctuary and the wider Dudhwa landscape. Photograph: (Sitangshu Das) Today, as cultivation has expanded closer to forest edges, those ancient paths increasingly overlap with human settlements. The Uttar Pradesh Forest Department, together with the Nature Environment & Wildlife Society (NEWS), launched the Gajmitra initiative in 2021. The Gajmitras are the first line of response whenever elephants approach human settlements. Through a year-long capacity-building programme, local residents from vulnerable villages were trained in elephant behaviour, conflict mitigation, early warning systems and safe response protocols before being inducted as Gajmitras. Today, more than 150 trained volunteers across villages such as Rampurwa, Matehi, Amba, Bishunapur, Bhawanipur and Bardia form a community-based early warning network that has transformed how elephant movement is managed in the region. The results are already visible. According to NEWS, the initiative helped reduce crop damage by nearly 70 percent over the past year. A second shift begins after dinner To understand what a full day, and especially a full night, looks like for the people safeguarding both villages and elephants, The Better India sat down with the Gajmitra rapid response team in Katarniaghat. Their work may resemble wildlife rescue from the outside, but the Gajmitras are farmers first. "We spend the day exactly like everyone else," says Suresh Kumar, one of the volunteers. "Our livelihood depends on farming. Only after finishing our work, eating dinner and making sure our families are settled do we prepare for elephant duty." Around 11 pm, teams of five disperse across villages bordering the forest. Two members of each team climb watchtowers overlooking likely elephant routes. Others patrol fields where fresh footprints were reported the previous evening. The Gajamitras coordinate with the local administration during unexpected human-wildlife encounters. Photograph: (Sitangshu Das) Every volunteer carries reflective jackets, whistles, torches, handheld sirens and megaphones. "If one team sees elephants, everyone is informed immediately," Suresh explains. "The Forest Department also joins us, and together we make sure villagers remain safe while giving the elephants enough space to move back towards the forest." "There hasn't been any need for tranquilisation or capturing elephants here," he says. "Most of our responsibility is observation, coordination and patience. If we can guide the elephants without creating panic, that is the best outcome." For the volunteers, success often means that by sunrise, there is nothing to report. ‘We go house to house’ Among the volunteers is Vineeta Devi, one of the earliest women to join the initiative. When the programme began in 2021, only four women enrolled. Even today, women make up only a small fraction of nearly 160 trained Gajmitras. For Vineeta, however, the work starts well before an elephant enters a village. "People ask why elephants come here," she says. "But these forests and corridors have belonged to elephants for generations. They continue to move between India and Nepal every year. What has changed is that our settlements now exist alongside those routes." Because social customs make overnight forest patrols difficult for many women, Vineeta's role centres on community preparedness inside the villages. "As soon as information comes in, we go from house to house telling families to stay indoors," she says. "Children are naturally curious, and adults often want to step outside to watch. Preventing crowds from gathering is one of the most important parts of our work because a calm elephant can become stressed if surrounded by people." Much of her time is devoted to awareness sessions held throughout the year. "Coexistence cannot begin only when an elephant is standing outside someone's field," she says. "Families need to understand elephant behaviour before that happens. If people know how to respond, many situations can be resolved without conflict ." Every night starts with one question For veteran volunteer Jaynarayan, the first question is always the same. Is it a family herd, or a solitary bull? "The response changes completely," he says. Family herds, led by experienced matriarchs, are usually focused on moving through the landscape with calves. Given enough space and careful guidance, they often continue along their route without prolonged confrontation. The members use whistles, reflector vests, megaphones, and alert networks to warn residents when elephant herds approach crop fields or residential boundaries. Photograph: (Sitangshu Das) A lone tusker requires a different approach. "They travel independently, cover long distances and are less predictable," Jaynarayan explains. "Simply making noise or flashing lights is not always enough. We have to be much more careful." Yet, he says, the greatest challenge often stands behind the volunteers rather than in front of them. "People want to watch, record videos or take photographs because seeing an elephant is exciting. We spend a lot of time asking people to move away. Crowd control becomes just as important as monitoring the elephant." Elephant sightings don’t end with the season Ashok Kumar has watched the landscape change over years of volunteering. Earlier, elephant sightings were largely seasonal. "Now we encounter them throughout the year," he says. He believes the explanation lies less with the elephants than with the changing landscape around them. "As forests become fragmented, elephants naturally spend more time near cultivated areas where food is abundant," he says. “It is easy to say elephant behaviour has changed, but we also have to recognise how much their surroundings have changed." Compensation exists, Ashok says, but coexistence cannot depend only on financial support. "Money can compensate for a damaged field," he says. "It cannot remove fear or uncertainty. The long-term solution is understanding why elephants use these landscapes and reducing situations where conflict begins." Success looks like a boring morning Most people never see the hours when the Gajmitras are at work. There are no cameras waiting in the darkness, and often no headlines the next morning. As sunrise washes over the Terai, the night's watch comes to an end. The torches are switched off, the reflective jackets tucked away, and the Gajmitras return to the fields they had left only a few hours earlier. By evening, they will do it all again. For these volunteers, success is measured by the number of nights that pass without fear, injury or loss. For them, coexistence is built through a routine repeated every night by farmers who have become guardians of a shared landscape.
